before.content_html:
What is Cellular Respiration?

Cellular respiration is a chemical process that takes place continuously in every living cell. It is not the same as breathing — respiration is a series of chemical reactions inside cells that transfer energy from glucose to a molecule called ATP (adenosine triphosphate). This energy powers everything cells do: muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, protein synthesis and active transport.

Respiration is an exothermic reaction — it releases energy to the surroundings. This is why your body generates heat, and why your temperature rises during exercise.

Key Fact

Cellular respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells — it is NOT breathing. It breaks down glucose and transfers the energy to ATP. It is exothermic, and occurs continuously in all living cells — animals, plants, fungi and bacteria alike.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and takes place mainly in the mitochondria. Because glucose is completely broken down, aerobic respiration yields a large amount of ATP — far more than anaerobic respiration. This is why organisms with high energy demands (such as muscles during sustained exercise) rely primarily on aerobic respiration.

The word equation is:

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$

The balanced symbol equation is:

$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O$$

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen supply cannot keep up with demand — for example, during intense exercise. Because glucose is not fully broken down, far less ATP is produced. In animals and humans, the product is lactic acid, which builds up in muscles causing the burning sensation of fatigue.

The word equation for anaerobic respiration in animals is:

$$\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$

In yeast (and other microorganisms), anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide — this process is called fermentation. The equations are:

$$\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$

Key Fact

Aerobic respiration produces a much larger ATP yield than anaerobic respiration because glucose is fully broken down. Anaerobic respiration in animals produces lactic acid; in yeast it produces ethanol + carbon dioxide (fermentation). Both types occur in the absence of sufficient oxygen.

After intense exercise, you continue to breathe heavily even though you have stopped moving. This is because your body needs extra oxygen to break down the lactic acid that accumulated during anaerobic respiration — this is called the oxygen debt. The liver converts lactic acid back to glucose using this extra oxygen. Heart rate and breathing rate remain elevated until all the lactic acid has been removed and the oxygen debt is repaid.

Mitochondria: The Cellular Power Stations

Mitochondria (singular: mitochondrion) are the site of aerobic respiration. They have two membranes: a smooth outer membrane and a highly folded inner membrane. The folds, called cristae, increase the surface area for the reactions of aerobic respiration to take place. Cells with high energy demands — muscle cells, liver cells, sperm cells — contain hundreds or thousands of mitochondria.

Mitochondria were first observed under light microscopes in the nineteenth century, but their function was unknown. Researchers working through the mid-twentieth century gradually worked out that these structures were the site of aerobic respiration by isolating them from cell homogenates and testing which reactions they could carry out. This is a good example of how scientific knowledge builds incrementally: first observation (structure), then experimental isolation (function), then detailed biochemical analysis of the reaction steps. Modern electron microscopy later revealed the cristae in detail, explaining why the surface area of the inner membrane is so large.

This progression from observation to mechanism illustrates a core principle of science: each new technique reveals a new level of detail, and earlier models are refined rather than discarded entirely.

Comparing Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration

It is important to be able to compare the two types of respiration clearly:

  • Oxygen required? Aerobic: yes. Anaerobic: no.
  • ATP yield: Aerobic: high. Anaerobic: low.
  • Products: Aerobic: CO₂ and water. Anaerobic: lactic acid (animals) or ethanol + CO₂ (yeast).
  • Location: Aerobic: mainly mitochondria. Anaerobic: cytoplasm.

Applications: Fermentation in Industry and Food

The process of fermentation by yeast is exploited in several industries. In bread-making, yeast ferments sugars in dough, producing carbon dioxide that causes the bread to rise (the ethanol evaporates during baking). In brewing and wine-making, yeast converts sugars in grains or grapes into ethanol. The fermentation must be carefully controlled: too little oxygen at the start limits yeast growth; too much will switch yeast to aerobic respiration, reducing ethanol yield.

Bacteria also carry out anaerobic respiration. Lactobacillus bacteria ferment lactose in milk to produce lactic acid — which lowers the pH and causes the milk proteins to coagulate, forming yoghurt and cheese. Understanding the biochemistry of respiration has allowed scientists to optimise these processes and, more recently, to develop biofuels such as bioethanol as more sustainable alternatives to fossil fuels.

Any two of the following (one mark each):

A student measures their breathing rate during rest, moderate exercise and intense exercise. The results show breathing rate is much higher during intense exercise and remains elevated for several minutes afterwards.
Explain why breathing rate stays elevated after intense exercise stops.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During intense exercise, oxygen supply cannot meet demand so anaerobic respiration occurs [1 mark]; lactic acid accumulates in muscles [1 mark]; after exercise, extra oxygen is needed to convert lactic acid back to glucose (oxygen debt) [1 mark]; breathing rate stays elevated to supply this extra oxygen until the debt is repaid [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why muscle cells contain many more mitochondria than skin cells. Use your knowledge of aerobic respiration in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Muscle cells contract frequently and require large amounts of ATP [1 mark]; aerobic respiration, which produces the most ATP, occurs in mitochondria [1 mark]; more mitochondria means more sites for aerobic respiration and more ATP can be produced to meet the high energy demand [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the above points clearly linked.
Developing: States muscles need more energy but does not connect to mitochondria number.
Emerging: Identifies that muscles need energy.

practice_questions.text: Compare the products and ATP yield of aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans. Explain the advantage of each type of respiration in different situations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering:
Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; large ATP yield; used during rest or sustained moderate exercise when oxygen is available [up to 3 marks].
Anaerobic: glucose → lactic acid; small ATP yield; used during intense exercise when oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough [up to 2 marks].
Evaluation: Each type has an advantage in its context — aerobic is efficient for sustained activity; anaerobic allows cells to keep working temporarily when oxygen is limiting [1 mark].
Secure: Both types described with correct products; advantage addressed for at least one.
Developing: One type described correctly.
Emerging: Vague reference to oxygen being needed for one type.

lessons.title: Growth, Stem Cells and Plant Hormones

before.content_html:
Cell Division and Growth

Multicellular organisms grow by increasing their number of cells through cell division and by increasing cell size. The type of cell division responsible for growth, repair and replacement of worn-out cells is mitosis. During mitosis, a cell first copies all of its DNA (so each chromosome exists in duplicate), then divides — one complete set of chromosomes goes to each daughter cell. The result is two cells genetically identical to the parent.

The cell cycle consists of two main phases: interphase (the long period of cell growth, DNA replication and organelle doubling) followed by mitosis and cell division. Most cells spend the vast majority of their time in interphase rather than actively dividing.

Key Fact

Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell. It is used for growth, repair of damaged tissue and replacement of ageing cells. Each daughter cell receives a full copy of the parent cell’s chromosomes.

Stem Cells: Undifferentiated and Versatile

Stem cells are cells that have not yet specialised. Unlike most body cells (which can only carry out one function), stem cells can divide repeatedly and then differentiate — change into a specialised cell type. There are two main categories:

  • Embryonic stem cells — found in the early embryo. They are pluripotent, meaning they can become almost any cell type in the body. This makes them highly useful for potential therapeutic applications.
  • Adult stem cells — found in specific tissues such as bone marrow and the lining of the gut. They are more restricted than embryonic stem cells and can only differentiate into a limited range of cell types. Bone marrow stem cells, for instance, produce red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

Stem cell therapy involves using stem cells to repair or replace damaged or diseased tissue. Bone marrow transplants are an established therapy — donor stem cells are transplanted into patients whose bone marrow has been destroyed (for example, by leukaemia treatment) to restore blood cell production. Researchers are also investigating using stem cells to replace insulin-producing cells in type 1 diabetes, restore nerve function after spinal cord injury, and repair heart muscle after a heart attack.

These potential applications are promising, but most are still in clinical trial stages. Risks include immune rejection of transplanted cells and the possibility that transplanted stem cells may divide uncontrollably, potentially causing cancer.

The Ethics of Stem Cell Research

This is a topic where scientific capability meets ethical judgement — a core example of the ‘Should we do this?’ question that science alone cannot answer. The debate around stem cell therapy centres on embryonic stem cells.

Key Fact

Arguments for using embryonic stem cells: could cure currently untreatable diseases; embryos used are typically surplus from IVF treatment (would otherwise be destroyed); potential to save many lives. Arguments against: the embryo is a potential human life and should not be used as a research tool; adult stem cells or induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) may offer alternatives; risks of uncontrolled cell division.

In the UK, research using human embryos is permitted up to 14 days after fertilisation and is regulated by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HFEA). This is an example of science being regulated through democratic and legal frameworks rather than being left entirely to scientific or commercial discretion.

Differentiation in Plants: Meristem Tissue

Unlike animals, in which differentiation is largely complete by adulthood, plants retain the ability to produce new cells throughout their lives. This is because plants have meristem tissue at their growing tips — both root tips and shoot tips. Meristem cells are essentially the plant equivalent of stem cells: they can divide repeatedly by mitosis and then differentiate into whatever cell type the growing plant needs (root hair cells, xylem vessels, leaf cells and so on).

This is why gardeners can take cuttings from plants and grow new, genetically identical plants from them. A cut stem has meristem tissue that can be stimulated to produce roots using rooting powder (which contains synthetic plant hormones), allowing the cutting to develop into a complete new plant. This technique is widely used in horticulture and agriculture to propagate high-quality varieties reliably.

Plant Hormones: Auxin and Tropisms

Auxin is a plant hormone produced at the growing tips of shoots. It controls how cells elongate: higher concentrations of auxin cause cells to elongate more. This leads to directional growth responses called tropisms.

In phototropism (growth response to light), auxin moves away from the light side of the shoot tip to the shaded side. The shaded side therefore has more auxin, causing its cells to elongate faster — the shoot bends towards the light. This is an adaptive response that maximises light capture for photosynthesis.

In gravitropism (growth response to gravity), auxin accumulates on the lower side of a root or shoot. In roots, high auxin concentrations inhibit elongation (roots are more sensitive to auxin), so the upper side elongates more and roots grow downward. In shoots, auxin promotes elongation, so shoots grow upward against gravity.

Synthetic versions of auxin are used as selective weedkillers: they cause broadleaf weeds to grow so rapidly that they die, while narrow-leaved grasses (including crops) are much less affected. Auxin-based rooting powders are used by horticulturalists to stimulate cuttings to form roots. Other plant hormones such as gibberellins are used to promote seed germination and fruit development in commercial horticulture.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells for growth, repair and cell replacement. The cell cycle involves interphase (DNA replication) followed by division.
  • Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and differentiate. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (almost any cell type); adult stem cells are more restricted. Stem cell therapy is promising but raises ethical questions about the status of embryos.
  • Auxin (Higher only) is a plant hormone that controls cell elongation. Uneven distribution of auxin causes phototropism and gravitropism, directing plant growth towards light and gravity respectively.
before.exam_tip_html: On ‘Evaluate’ questions about stem cell therapy, remember to address both the risks and the benefits, and to acknowledge that the use of embryonic stem cells involves an ethical judgement — not just a scientific one. For auxin and tropisms (Higher only), always explain the mechanism: auxin moves to one side → cells on that side elongate more → the plant bends. Simply stating “auxin causes bending” without the mechanism will not earn full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a stem cell?
A) A specialised cell that can only carry out one function
B) An undifferentiated cell that can divide and become different cell types
C) A cell found only in the nervous system
D) A cell that has stopped dividing permanently
practice_questions.marks: B) An undifferentiated cell that can divide and become different cell types [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between embryonic stem cells and adult stem cells.
practice_questions.marks: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (can become almost any cell type) [1 mark]; adult stem cells are more restricted and can only differentiate into a limited range of cell types [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how auxin causes a shoot to bend towards light. (Higher only)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Auxin is produced at the shoot tip and migrates to the shaded side [1 mark]; higher auxin concentration causes cells on the shaded side to elongate more [1 mark]; unequal growth causes the shoot to bend towards the light [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three mechanistic steps above.
Developing: States auxin moves to one side but does not explain cell elongation.

Mastering:
Benefits: embryonic stem cells are pluripotent and could be directed to become insulin-producing (beta) cells [1 mark]; could restore normal blood glucose control without the need for daily insulin injections [1 mark]; embryos used are typically surplus from IVF treatment [1 mark].
Risks/ethical concerns: embryos are potential human lives and using them raises ethical objections [1 mark]; risk of immune rejection of transplanted cells [1 mark]; stem cells may divide uncontrollably (cancer risk) [1 mark].
Conclusion: A balanced statement weighing scientific potential against ethical concerns.
Secure: Both benefits and concerns addressed; conclusion present.

Emerging: Vague reference to stem cells being useful or controversial.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a higher concentration of auxin inhibits root growth but promotes shoot growth. (Higher only)

Mastering: Roots are more sensitive to auxin than shoots [1 mark]; in roots, high auxin inhibits cell elongation, so the side with more auxin grows less and the root bends towards higher auxin (downward) [1 mark]; in shoots, the same high concentration promotes cell elongation [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three points.
Developing: States roots and shoots respond differently but without mechanistic detail.
Emerging: Vague statement about auxin and growth.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes osmosis?
A) The movement of all molecules from high to low concentration using energy
B) The net movement of water from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
C) The movement of glucose against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins
D) The random movement of particles in all directions equally
practice_questions.marks: B) The net movement of water from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which active transport differs from diffusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following:
• Active transport requires energy (from respiration); diffusion does not [1 mark]
• Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient; diffusion moves with the gradient [1 mark]
• Active transport uses carrier proteins in the membrane; diffusion does not require carrier proteins [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the alveoli are adapted to maximise the rate of gas exchange.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Large surface area provided by millions of alveoli [1 mark]; walls only one cell thick, minimising diffusion distance [1 mark]; rich capillary blood supply continuously removes oxygen and delivers carbon dioxide, maintaining steep concentration gradients [1 mark]; moist lining allows gases to dissolve before diffusing across the membrane [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four adaptations, each linked to diffusion rate.
Developing: One or two adaptations named without mechanistic link to diffusion.
Emerging: Vague reference to lungs being good at gas exchange.

practice_questions.text:
A student places a piece of potato in a concentrated salt solution and a second piece in pure water. After 30 minutes, the potato in salt solution has decreased in mass and the potato in water has increased in mass.
Explain these results using your knowledge of osmosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The salt solution is more concentrated than the potato cell contents [1 mark]; water moves out of the potato cells by osmosis (down the water potential gradient) into the salt solution [1 mark]; cells lose water, causing the potato to decrease in mass [1 mark]. In water, the solution is more dilute than the cell contents; water moves into the potato cells by osmosis, increasing their mass [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four points.
Developing: Correct direction for one condition, without explanation in terms of water potential.
Emerging: States water moves in or out without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain why root hair cells require active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil, whereas oxygen moves into blood by diffusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mineral ions are present in very low concentrations in the soil but in higher concentration inside the root hair cell [1 mark]; so minerals must be moved against the concentration gradient, which requires energy from respiration via active transport [1 mark]; oxygen, by contrast, is at higher concentration in the alveoli than in the blood, so it can move down its gradient by diffusion without energy [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three points.
Developing: States active transport requires energy without connecting to concentration gradient comparison.
Emerging: Names both processes but does not explain the distinction.

practice_questions.text: Explain the advantages of the double circulatory system over a single circulatory system in meeting the high metabolic demands of mammals.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit [1 mark]; the pulmonary circuit (heart to lungs) replenishes oxygen and removes CO₂ [1 mark]; the systemic circuit (heart to body) delivers oxygenated blood at high pressure to all tissues [1 mark]; separating the two circuits means blood is re-pressurised after passing through the lungs, so it reaches tissues at high pressure [1 mark]; high pressure means faster delivery of oxygen and glucose to active cells, sustaining high metabolic rates [1 mark]; a single circulation would have low pressure reaching the body after passing through the lungs, insufficient for active mammals [1 mark].
Secure: Four or five points clearly explained.
Developing: Describes the two circuits without explaining the pressure advantage.
Emerging: States blood goes to the lungs and body.

before.exam_tip_html: When explaining diffusion or osmosis in a biological context, always name the direction of movement relative to the concentration gradient and state whether energy is required. For alveoli adaptation questions, link each adaptation directly to a factor that increases diffusion rate — e.g. “thin walls reduce the diffusion distance, increasing the rate of gas exchange.” Describing active transport: you must mention the concentration gradient is reversed AND that energy from respiration is required.

before.content_html:
Structure of the Nervous System

The human nervous system allows the body to detect changes in the environment and produce coordinated responses. It has two main divisions:

  • Central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord. This is the processing centre: it receives information from receptors, interprets it and sends out instructions to effectors.
  • Peripheral nervous system — the nerves that extend from the CNS to the rest of the body. These include sensory neurones (carrying signals to the CNS) and motor neurones (carrying signals from the CNS to muscles and glands).
Key Fact

The nervous response pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (CNS) → motor neurone → effector → response. The CNS (brain and spinal cord) is the coordination centre in the middle of every voluntary response.

Neurones and Their Structure

There are three types of neurone:

  • Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS.
  • Relay neurones are found within the CNS and connect sensory neurones to motor neurones.
  • Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles, which contract, or glands, which secrete).

All neurones have a cell body (containing the nucleus), dendrites (short extensions that receive impulses) and a long axon that transmits impulses away from the cell body. Many axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath — an insulating fatty layer that speeds up the transmission of electrical impulses.

Neurones do not physically touch each other. The tiny gap between two neurones is called a synapse. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of one neurone, it triggers the release of chemical messengers called neurotransmitters into the synaptic gap. These molecules diffuse across the gap and bind to receptor proteins on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse there.

Synapses are important because they allow signals to pass in only one direction (neurotransmitters are released from one side only), and because they allow the nervous system to integrate information from many inputs before deciding whether to generate a response. Many drugs and toxins work by interfering with synaptic transmission — for example, some drugs mimic neurotransmitters, while others block their receptors.

Reflex Actions

A reflex action is an automatic, rapid response to a stimulus that bypasses conscious thought. Reflexes protect the body from harm — for example, pulling your hand away from a hot surface, blinking when something approaches your eye, or the pupil reflex in bright light.

The pathway for a reflex is called the reflex arc. In a spinal reflex, the relay neurone is in the spinal cord rather than the brain, which is why reflexes are so fast — the signal does not need to travel all the way to the brain for a decision to be made.

Key Fact

Reflex arcs bypass the brain — the relay neurone is in the spinal cord — making reflexes faster than voluntary actions. This speed is crucial: reflexes protect us from harm before we have time to think. Examples include withdrawing from pain and the pupil light reflex.

The Reflex Arc: Step by Step

Using the example of pulling your hand away from a hot surface:

  1. A receptor in the skin (a thermoreceptor) detects the intense heat stimulus.
  2. An impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord.
  3. In the spinal cord, the impulse crosses a synapse and passes along a relay neurone.
  4. The relay neurone crosses another synapse and triggers a motor neurone.
  5. The impulse reaches the effector (the bicep muscle in the arm), which contracts.
  6. The response: the hand is pulled away. Simultaneously, a signal is sent to the brain so you become conscious of the event — but this happens after the response has already occurred.

When bright light shines into the eye, the pupil automatically constricts (gets smaller) to protect the sensitive retina. This is the pupil light reflex. Light-sensitive receptors in the retina send signals along sensory neurones to the brain stem; motor signals return along motor neurones to the circular muscles of the iris, causing them to contract and the pupil to narrow. In dim light, the opposite occurs: radial muscles contract and the pupil dilates to allow more light in.

The pupil reflex is coordinated in the brain stem rather than the spinal cord — it is still a reflex (automatic) but its relay station is higher up the nervous system. Doctors use this reflex to assess brain function: an absence of the pupil reflex after a head injury may indicate serious brain damage.

The Brain: Regions and Functions

The brain is the master coordination centre of the nervous system. It is made up of billions of interconnected neurones and is divided into distinct regions, each associated with particular functions. The cerebrum is the largest region and controls conscious thought, memory, language and voluntary movement. The cerebellum coordinates balance and the precision of movement. The medulla oblongata controls automatic (unconscious) functions such as heart rate and breathing rate.

Understanding the brain remains one of the biggest challenges in science. Techniques such as MRI scanning allow scientists to observe which brain regions are active during different tasks, but the complexity of billions of neurones interacting makes a full understanding difficult. Investigations into brain function are constrained by ethical limits on what experiments can be performed on living human subjects, by individual variation between brains, and by the fact that damage to one brain region may produce different effects in different people. This is an ongoing area of scientific investigation where models are continually refined as new evidence emerges.

glossary_terms.definition: The organ system that detects stimuli and coordinates rapid responses, consisting of the brain, spinal cord and a network of nerves.
A specialised cell that transmits electrical impulses. There are three types: sensory, relay and motor neurones, each with a distinct structure and function.
Specialised cells that detect a specific type of stimulus — such as light, pressure, temperature, sound or chemicals — and convert it into an electrical signal.
An organ (muscle or gland) that carries out a response when stimulated by a motor neurone. Muscles contract; glands secrete substances.
The microscopic gap between two neurones where chemical neurotransmitters carry signals from one neurone to the next.
A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve a conscious decision. Reflexes protect the body from harm and are faster than voluntary responses.
The pathway through which a reflex response travels: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector.
The largest region of the brain, responsible for conscious thought, memory, learning, language, voluntary movement and the interpretation of sensory information.
The region of the brain at the back that coordinates balance and fine motor control, ensuring smooth and precise movement.
The part of the brain that connects the brain to the spinal cord and controls unconscious vital functions such as heart rate and breathing rate.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the function of a relay neurone?
A) It carries impulses from a receptor to the CNS
B) It connects sensory neurones to motor neurones within the CNS
C) It carries impulses from the CNS to a muscle or gland
D) It releases neurotransmitters into the bloodstream
practice_questions.marks: B) It connects sensory neurones to motor neurones within the CNS [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a reflex action and give one example.
practice_questions.marks: A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought [1 mark]; example: withdrawing from pain / blinking / pupil constriction in bright light [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how a signal crosses a synapse. Include the role of neurotransmitters in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: An electrical impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone [1 mark]; neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic gap [1 mark]; they diffuse across and bind to receptor proteins on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three steps.
Developing: Mentions neurotransmitters crossing the gap but lacks the receptor-binding step.
Emerging: Vague reference to chemicals carrying signals.

practice_questions.text: A student touches a hot pan and immediately withdraws their hand before feeling pain. Using the reflex arc, explain why their hand moved before they felt pain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The reflex arc uses a relay neurone in the spinal cord [1 mark]; the motor signal to the hand muscles is sent from the spinal cord directly (without waiting for the brain to process the signal) [1 mark]; the hand withdraws before the sensory signal has time to travel all the way to the brain and produce a conscious experience of pain [1 mark]; a separate signal does travel to the brain after the reflex, which is when pain is felt [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four points.
Developing: States the reflex bypasses the brain but without mechanistic detail.
Emerging: Correctly states the hand moves before feeling pain without scientific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the structure of a myelinated axon is adapted to transmit impulses more rapidly.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The myelin sheath is a fatty insulating layer around the axon [1 mark]; it prevents electrical signals from leaking across the axon membrane [1 mark]; this means the impulse jumps between gaps in the sheath (nodes of Ranvier), travelling much faster than in an unmyelinated axon [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three points.
Developing: States myelin insulates the axon but does not explain how this speeds transmission.
Emerging: Identifies myelin as an insulator.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of reflex actions to human survival. Consider both the advantages and any situations where reflexes could be disadvantageous.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering:
Advantages: Reflexes are much faster than voluntary responses so they protect the body from harm before damage occurs [1 mark]; they are automatic, so no mental energy is required — voluntary attention is freed for other tasks [1 mark]; examples: withdrawing from pain, pupil reflex preventing retinal damage [1 mark].
Disadvantages / limitations: Reflexes cannot be adapted to context — a reflex response may occur even when it is not the best action [1 mark]; conditioned reflexes can be overridden with practice (e.g. a trained surgeon controls their startle reflex), suggesting reflexes are not entirely automatic [1 mark].
Conclusion: Overall, reflexes are highly beneficial for survival by providing instant protection, outweighing occasional cases where an automatic response is unhelpful [1 mark].
Secure: Both advantages and limitations addressed, conclusion present.
Developing: Advantages only, limited analysis.
Emerging: States reflexes are fast and helpful without further development.

before.exam_tip_html: For reflex arc questions, examiners want the components in the correct order — write the full sequence: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector. A very common error is omitting the relay neurone. When explaining why reflexes are faster than voluntary actions, always state that the relay neurone is in the spinal cord, so the signal does not need to travel all the way to the brain before a response is sent. For synapse questions, describe three steps: impulse arrives → neurotransmitters released into the gap → bind to receptors on next neurone → new impulse generated.
before.description: Sensors, neurones and how reflexes protect us from harm. Key concepts and applications explained.

before.content_html:
Homeostasis and Hormonal Control

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment. Many homeostatic systems in the body use hormones — chemical messengers produced by glands and transported in the blood to target organs. Hormonal responses are slower than nervous responses but longer-lasting, making them well-suited for regulating sustained processes like blood glucose concentration and water balance.

Homeostatic control works through negative feedback: when a condition deviates from the normal range, the body detects the change and triggers a response that reverses it, returning conditions to the set point. This is how the body maintains blood glucose, temperature and water levels.

Key Fact

All homeostatic systems have three components: receptor (detects the change), coordination centre (processes the information — e.g. the pancreas or brain) and effector (brings about the corrective response). The system operates by negative feedback, reversing any deviation from the normal range.

Blood Glucose Regulation

Blood glucose concentration is controlled by the pancreas. When blood glucose rises after a meal, the pancreas secretes insulin. Insulin causes:

  • Body cells (especially muscle and liver cells) to take up glucose from the blood.
  • The liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen for storage (glycogenesis).

Blood glucose falls back to normal. If glucose stays too high, the condition is called diabetes mellitus.

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. No insulin is produced, so blood glucose cannot be lowered. Management requires regular insulin injections or an insulin pump, and careful monitoring of carbohydrate intake.

Type 2 diabetes occurs when body cells become less sensitive (resistant) to insulin. The pancreas still produces insulin, but it is less effective. Risk factors include being overweight, physical inactivity and diet. It can often be managed through lifestyle changes (diet and exercise), though medication may also be prescribed. Type 2 diabetes is far more common than type 1 and is strongly linked to lifestyle factors, though genetic susceptibility also plays a role.

Glucagon and the Full Negative Feedback Loop

When blood glucose falls below the normal range (e.g. during exercise or fasting), the pancreas secretes glucagon. Glucagon stimulates the liver to convert stored glycogen back into glucose (glycogenolysis), raising blood glucose back to normal. This completes the negative feedback loop: insulin lowers glucose, glucagon raises it — together they maintain the blood glucose within a narrow normal range.

Water Balance and the Kidney

The body also regulates its water content through the kidneys. The kidneys filter blood and adjust how much water is reabsorbed into the blood before producing urine. This process is controlled by ADH (anti-diuretic hormone).

Key Fact

ADH is released by the pituitary gland when blood water potential falls (e.g. after sweating or not drinking enough). ADH travels in the blood to the kidneys, where it makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water. More water is reabsorbed into the blood, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. As water potential returns to normal, ADH secretion decreases — a classic negative feedback loop.

The Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle is a roughly 28-day hormonal cycle that prepares the uterus for possible pregnancy. It is controlled by four key hormones, all interacting through feedback mechanisms:

  • FSH — released by the pituitary gland. It causes an egg to mature in the ovary and stimulates the ovary to produce oestrogen.
  • Oestrogen — produced by the ovaries. It thickens the uterus lining and, at high levels, stimulates a surge of LH while inhibiting FSH.
  • LH — the surge of LH triggers ovulation (release of the mature egg) around day 14.
  • Progesterone — produced by the empty follicle after ovulation. It maintains the uterus lining. If no fertilisation occurs, progesterone levels drop, the lining breaks down, and menstruation begins.

Hormonal contraceptives (the pill, injection, implant or patch) prevent pregnancy by maintaining elevated levels of oestrogen and/or progesterone. This inhibits the release of FSH and LH from the pituitary gland, preventing follicle maturation and ovulation. Without ovulation, there is no egg to fertilise. Some hormonal contraceptives also thicken the cervical mucus, making it harder for sperm to reach any egg, and thin the uterus lining, making implantation less likely.

Thermoregulation: Maintaining Body Temperature

As well as blood glucose and water balance, the body must maintain a core temperature of around 37°C — the optimum for most human enzymes. The hypothalamus in the brain acts as the body’s thermostat, detecting changes in blood temperature and coordinating corrective responses.

When body temperature rises too high (e.g. during exercise or in hot weather):

  • Vasodilation — blood vessels near the skin surface widen (vasodilate), increasing blood flow to the skin so heat can be lost by radiation.
  • Sweating — sweat glands release sweat onto the skin surface. As sweat evaporates, it takes energy (heat) from the skin, cooling the body.

When body temperature falls too low (e.g. in cold conditions):

  • Vasoconstriction — blood vessels near the skin narrow, reducing blood flow to the skin and conserving heat for vital organs.
  • Shivering — rapid, involuntary muscle contractions generate heat through increased respiration.

Both responses return body temperature to the set point by negative feedback — once temperature is restored, the hypothalamus switches off the corrective responses.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Homeostasis uses negative feedback. Blood glucose is regulated by insulin (lowers glucose, stimulates glycogen storage) and glucagon (Higher: raises glucose, stimulates glycogenolysis). Type 1 diabetes is caused by destruction of insulin-producing cells; type 2 involves reduced insulin sensitivity.
  • ADH (Higher) is released by the pituitary gland when blood water potential falls. It increases water reabsorption in the kidneys, producing concentrated urine and restoring water balance by negative feedback.
  • The menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH (matures egg, stimulates oestrogen), oestrogen (thickens lining, triggers LH surge), LH (triggers ovulation at day 14) and progesterone (maintains lining after ovulation). Hormonal contraception works by inhibiting FSH and LH to prevent ovulation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the role of insulin?
A) It raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to convert glycogen to glucose
B) It lowers blood glucose by stimulating cells to take up glucose and the liver to store it as glycogen
C) It is released by the pituitary gland in response to low blood glucose
D) It prevents ovulation by inhibiting FSH and LH
practice_questions.marks: B) It lowers blood glucose by stimulating cells to take up glucose and the liver to store it as glycogen [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks: Type 1: the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, so no insulin is produced [1 mark]; type 2: body cells become less sensitive/resistant to insulin, so it has less effect [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of ADH in regulating water balance. (Higher only)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: When blood water potential falls, the pituitary gland releases ADH [1 mark]; ADH travels to the kidneys and makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water [1 mark]; more water is reabsorbed into the blood, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine, restoring water potential by negative feedback [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three steps.
Developing: States ADH causes kidneys to reabsorb water but lacks the trigger and feedback.
Emerging: Names ADH without explaining its mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the four hormones of the menstrual cycle interact to produce ovulation around day 14.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: FSH from the pituitary gland causes follicle maturation in the ovary and stimulates oestrogen production [1 mark]; oestrogen causes the uterus lining to thicken and, at high levels, triggers a surge of LH [1 mark]; the LH surge triggers ovulation (release of the egg) at around day 14 [1 mark]; progesterone is then produced by the empty follicle to maintain the lining; if no fertilisation occurs, progesterone falls and menstruation begins [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four mechanisms.
Developing: Names the hormones without linking them in sequence.
Emerging: States ovulation occurs at day 14 without hormonal explanation.

practice_questions.text: A patient with type 1 diabetes tests their blood glucose before breakfast and finds it is well above the normal range, despite not having eaten. Explain why blood glucose can be high in type 1 diabetes even without eating, and describe how the patient could lower it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In type 1 diabetes, no insulin is produced [1 mark]; overnight, the liver still converts glycogen to glucose and releases it into the blood (normal background glucose release) [1 mark]; without insulin, cells cannot take up this glucose and the liver cannot store it as glycogen [1 mark]; blood glucose therefore rises; the patient would inject insulin to stimulate glucose uptake by cells [1 mark]; they should also monitor carbohydrate intake and exercise levels, as both affect blood glucose [1 mark].
Secure: Four of the five points.
Developing: States no insulin is made and injection is needed, without mechanistic explanation.
Emerging: Identifies type 1 as lacking insulin.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of hormonal contraception to control fertility. In your answer, consider how it works, its effectiveness and any ethical considerations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering:
Mechanism: maintains high levels of oestrogen and/or progesterone, inhibiting FSH and LH release, preventing ovulation [up to 2 marks].
Benefits: highly effective when used correctly; some forms are long-acting (implant, injection) and do not require daily action; can also reduce symptoms of conditions like endometriosis [1 mark].
Limitations/risks: does not protect against sexually transmitted infections; some individuals experience side effects (mood changes, nausea, blood clot risk for some types); ethical objection from some religious or personal viewpoints about using hormones to prevent natural fertility [up to 2 marks].
Conclusion: Weighs effectiveness against risks and ethical concerns [1 mark].
Secure: Mechanism plus benefits and one concern.
Developing: Mechanism described only.
Emerging: Vague reference to the pill preventing pregnancy.
